summary.text: Freezing rain is rain chilled below freezing on its way down that turns to ice the moment it hits a surface.
It forms when falling snow melts in a warm layer aloft, then the rain passes through a freezing layer near the ground too shallow for it to freeze.
The resulting glaze ice can build up several centimeters thick, breaking tree limbs, downing power lines and making roads dangerous.

items.prompt: Snow melts into rain in a warm layer high up, then falls through a very deep layer of below-freezing air near the ground. What most likely lands?

options.label: Freezing rain
Ordinary rain
Ice pellets (sleet)
Hail

items.explain: If the freezing layer is deep enough, the drops have time to freeze into ice pellets before reaching the ground; a shallow layer gives freezing rain.

items.prompt: After an ice storm, a branch is wrapped in one smooth, thick shell of ice. Why does the ice take the branch's shape?

options.label: Snow piles up and slowly melts into it
It arrives as liquid drops that conform to it
Ice pellets fuse together as they land
Frost grows outward from inside the wood

items.explain: Freezing rain hits as rain droplets rather than ice pellets, so it conforms to the object's shape and builds one thick layer of glaze.

items.prompt: Why is a road glazed by freezing rain harder to drive on than a snowy one?

options.label: Wet ice gives almost no traction
The ice is far thicker than snow
The ice hides potholes in the road
The ice is always freshly falling

items.explain: Unlike snow, wet ice provides almost no traction, so vehicles slide even on gentle slopes.

items.prompt: A forecaster needs to be sure freezing rain is actually falling in a certain town. What gives direct confirmation?

options.label: A Doppler weather radar image
A computer forecast model
A dual-polarized radar scan
Reports from ground weather stations

items.explain: Radar can only estimate freezing rain indirectly; surface observations by staffed or automatic stations are the only direct confirmation.

items.prompt: Which stack of air layers, from the clouds down, sets up freezing rain?

options.label: A warm layer aloft over a thin freezing layer at the ground
Below-freezing air all the way from cloud to ground
Above-freezing air all the way from cloud to ground
A warm layer aloft over a deep freezing layer below

items.explain: Snow melts in the warm layer aloft, and if the freezing layer at the surface is very shallow, the drops reach the ground still liquid but supercooled.

items.prompt: Freezing rain is especially dangerous for aircraft. What does the ice do to a plane?

options.label: It freezes the fuel in the tanks
It reshapes the wings and control surfaces
It cuts off radio contact with the ground
It cracks the cockpit windows

items.explain: The ice can effectively remould the shape of the airfoil and the flight control surfaces.

paragraphs.heading: Rain that turns to ice on contact
paragraphs.text: Freezing rain is rain kept below freezing by the cold air around it, so it ices over the moment it touches something. Unlike a mix of rain with snow or ice pellets, it is made only of liquid drops. The drops become supercooled, meaning chilled below freezing while still liquid, as they fall through a cold layer of air hundreds of meters up. They then freeze on whatever they strike: the ground, trees, power lines, aircraft and cars. The ice that results, called glaze ice, can grow several centimeters thick and coat every exposed surface.

paragraphs.heading: Snow, then rain, then ice
paragraphs.text: In the classic route, it starts as snow that falls into a layer of warm air aloft, often near the 800 mbar level, where it melts into rain. The rain then drops through a layer of below-freezing air just above the ground and cools under 0 °C. If that cold layer is deep, the drops can freeze into ice pellets, or sleet, before they land. If it is very shallow, they reach the ground still liquid, as supercooled rain. Studies also describe a second route, in which drops form as liquid and stay unfrozen until they touch a surface at or below 0 °C.

paragraphs.heading: The weather setup
paragraphs.text: Freezing rain often comes with an approaching warm front, when cold air is trapped near the ground while warm air is carried in above it. In North America this happens, for example, when a low pressure system travels during the cold season out of the Mississippi River Valley toward the Appalachians and the Saint Lawrence River Valley, with a strong high pressure system further east. This pattern is called cold-air damming, and it brings very cold, dry air at the surface under the high. Warm air from the Gulf of Mexico often feeds the freezing precipitation.

paragraphs.heading: Spotting it on radar
paragraphs.text: Only observers or automatic stations on the ground can confirm freezing rain directly, since no weather radar shows the type of precipitation itself. Radar can still mark out the likely area. Where snow is melting, the wet flakes are still large and coated in water, so they send back a much stronger echo, a feature called the brightband. That band shows a warm layer above the ground where snow melts, which can mean rain below, or freezing rain if the surface is under freezing. A dual-polarized radar, which sends out both vertical and horizontal waves, can compare the two returns to work out the shape of what it sees and so the type of precipitation.

paragraphs.heading: When the ice gets heavy
paragraphs.text: A storm that leaves a thick coat of glaze ice is called an ice storm. These storms are not especially violent, and light, brief freezing rain leaves only thin ice and minor damage, such as clearing dead branches from trees. When a lot builds up, though, it becomes one of the most dangerous winter hazards. Once the ice passes about 6.4 mm (0.25 in), heavily coated tree limbs can snap and fall onto power lines, and iced lines grow so heavy that poles, insulators and wires break, cutting off power. Wind and lightning, when present, make the damage worse.

paragraphs.heading: Roads and wings
paragraphs.text: Because freezing rain lands as a droplet rather than as an ice pellet, it molds itself to the shape of the ground, a branch or a car, building one thick layer of glaze. On roads that is treacherous: unlike snow, wet ice gives almost no grip, so vehicles slide even on gentle slopes. It is also very dangerous for aircraft, because the ice can change the shape of the wings and flight control surfaces.
